content: The Guide for Establishing a Pathology Laboratory in the Context of Cancer Control, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2019, provides a comprehensive framework for setting up and maintaining pathology laboratories, particularly in the context of cancer diagnosis and management. This guide emphasizes the critical role of pathology services in cancer control, as they are essential for accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and monitoring of outcomes. Without reliable pathology services, effective cancer treatment cannot be delivered. Pathology services are integral to cancer control programs, as they enable the identification of malignant diseases and the determination of histopathological features, such as tumor type, grade, and extent. Cytopathology, for example, is widely used for cancer screening, diagnosis, and surveillance. It is estimated that 70% of all medical decisions are based on laboratory diagnoses, underscoring the importance of pathology and laboratory medicine (PALM) in guiding treatment, informing prognosis, and ensuring optimal patient care. The guide highlights the global burden of cancer, with 18 million new cases and 10 million deaths annually as of 2018, a number projected to rise to 30 million new cases by 2040. Despite the critical importance of pathology services, there is a significant gap in access to these services worldwide, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). While 95% of high-income countries report general availability of pathology services, only 26% of low-income countries can claim the same. This disparity is attributed to factors such as under-resourced laboratories, a lack of trained personnel, inadequate equipment, and poor quality management systems. The guide outlines the minimum requirements for establishing a pathology laboratory, including histopathology and cytopathology services, and provides recommendations for addressing common barriers to access. These barriers include insufficient leadership and governance, lack of infrastructure, inadequate human resources, weak service delivery, and limited financing. The guide also stresses the importance of national laboratory policies, strategic planning, and stakeholder engagement in overcoming these challenges. Pathology services consist of three main phases: pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical. Each phase involves specific components, such as specimen collection, processing, staining, and reporting. Proper specimen handling, fixation, and labeling are critical to ensuring accurate diagnoses. The guide also emphasizes the importance of comprehensive pathology reports, which should include diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive information. Synoptic reporting, a structured method of documentation, is recommended to improve consistency, reduce errors, and streamline clinical workflows. Additionally, the guide addresses the retention and archiving of patient data and specimens, which are essential for future testing, second opinions, and medico-legal purposes. To establish a pathology laboratory, the process begins with a situation analysis of national policies, regulatory frameworks, and the needs of the target population. Stakeholder engagement, including input from hospital management, clinical departments, and laboratory staff, is crucial. Tools such as the WHO Laboratory Assessment Tool can assist in evaluating existing laboratory systems and identifying areas for improvement. In summary, the WHO guide provides a detailed roadmap for establishing and strengthening pathology laboratories to support cancer control efforts. It underscores the need for reliable pathology services to improve access to timely and accurate diagnoses, which are essential for effective cancer prevention, treatment, and care. By addressing the challenges and implementing the recommendations outlined in the guide, countries can enhance their capacity to manage the growing burden of cancer and achieve better health outcomes.
